name: Dayak (Ngaju)
confidence_why: Hardeland's 1858 grammar and Mihing and Stokhof's 1977 phonology of the Pulau Petak dialect both place word stress on the penultimate syllable, but Kaufman and Himmelmann (2024) report the impression, offered without data, that Ngaju shows even prominence across syllables and may lack word stress altogether. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Hardeland 1858.

Wo indess, in durch Suffixe abgeleiteten Wörtern, diese Hauptsylbe zur drittletzten Sylbe wird, bleibt der Accent doch auf der Penultima

new_statements.quote: The distribution of the stressless Java prototype has yet to be investigated systematically, as it has only recently gained acceptance as an independent type. [...] It is unclear whether many Malayic languages of Borneo and Sumatra also belong to this type. Ngaju Dayak in Central Kalimantan, impressionistically, at least, appears to show remarkably even prominence across syllables. Tadmor (2000) posits that lack of lexical accent is a general western feature that extends through Sumatra and Borneo. It seems, however, that Sumatra and Borneo show considerable variation, in addition to ongoing changes induced by contact with varieties of Malay.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2 record 'StressTyp2') gives Ngaju a fixed penultimate rule (penultimate stress). Kaufman & Himmelmann instead suggest, impressionistically, that Ngaju Dayak has no word stress at all (even prominence across syllables, stressless 'Java prototype'). That is a different type (stressless vs. fixed penult), though the authors present it as an unverified impression.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The authors tentatively place Ngaju Dayak in their 'Java prototype' (languages without word-based stress): on their own auditory impression the syllables of a word show remarkably even prominence, i.e. no syllable is singled out as stressed. The statement is explicitly impressionistic and hedged ('impressionistically, at least, appears'), not based on instrumental or systematic data; the chapter as a whole argues that prominence in such languages is phrasal, not lexical.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Ngaju; the authors add that Sumatra and Borneo 'show considerable variation' and ongoing contact-induced change from Malay, so the placement in the stressless type is provisional.
new_statements.identity_note: Kaufman & Himmelmann refer to 'Ngaju Dayak in Central Kalimantan' generally, no dialect named. Ristati 2006 is on Dayak Ngaju without dialect specification in the abstract. Iper et al. 1998 (not opened) is about Katingan, a related variety along the Katingan river that the 1991 and 2013 Ngaju grammars held by the project treat as a separate neighbouring language/dialect area ('bahasa Katingan'); any stress statement from it would be about Katingan, not Ngaju proper.

new_statements.translation: [key, p.95] [^] = fairly strong stress, [`] = medium stress ... [p.96] Disyllabic words generally receive fairly-strong and medium stress, as in the following examples: [etâŋ] 'basket', [tùnîs] 'quiet', [mètûh] 'medium', [òmbât] 'why', [tìmbÊn] 'too (much)' ... Trisyllabic words generally receive fairly-strong and medium stress: [kàwìlâp] 'lath', [bàgàmbûh] 'greedy', [bàsèpût] 'fat', [hàntùÊn] 'kuntilanak ghost' ... [p.97] The stress applied to four-syllable words is generally medium moving toward fairly strong: [tàbàlîÈn] 'ironwood', [kùwàltûtàl] 'stammering', [kàmàsârày] 'lemongrass', [jàlàtîÈn] 'nine' ... Based on the data obtained, no meaning-distinguishing (distinctive) stress is found in Katingan. (Conclusion p.135: although stress, pitch and juncture can be identified in Katingan, no suprasegmental element that distinguishes meaning was found.)

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2) records Dayak (Ngaju) as fixed penult (penultimate stress). This monograph, on the Katingan variety (dialek Ngawa, lower Katingan River; retired ISO [kxg], merged into Ngaju [nij] in 2008, Glottolog files the reference under ngaj1237), marks the strongest stress on the FINAL syllable of all two- and three-syllable roots and on the penult only in four-syllable roots, and states stress is non-distinctive. Placement therefore differs from the catalog for the common word shapes; it matches penult only for 4-syllable roots. Caveat on identity: it is a dialect description, not standard (Kapuas/Kahayan) Ngaju, and the description is impressionistic (four auditory degrees, no a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Domain is the root word (kata dasar). The prose gives only degrees of stress per word length, not a position; the position is read off the diacritics, which are consistent: monosyllables carry strong stress if exclamations, otherwise fairly strong; in every marked two- and three-syllable root the strongest mark (fairly strong, ^) sits on the FINAL syllable with medium (`) on the preceding syllable(s); in the (rare, 'very limited') four-syllable roots the fairly-strong mark sits on the PENULT with medium on the others. Stress is explicitly non-distinctive (pp. 97, 135). So: word-final prominence for the ordinary 2-3-syllable root, penult in 4-syllable roots, non-contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Non-final syllables of 2-3-syllable roots are marked 'sedang' (medium), i.e. a weaker degree on every pre-tonic syllable rather than an alternating secondary stress; in 4-syllable roots all syllables other than the penult carry the medium mark.
new_statements.exceptions: Four-syllable roots (said to be very few) carry the fairly-strong mark on the penult, not the final ([tàbàlîÈn], [kùwàltûtàl], [kàmàsârày], [jàlàtîÈn], [hàràmâUŋ]); monosyllabic exclamations take the strong degree. One disyllable, [etâŋ], is printed with only the final-syllable mark. No statement about affixed words (discussion limited to roots).
new_statements.identity_note: Work 0 describes bahasa Katingan dialek Ngawa (lower Katingan River: Kecamatan Katingan Hilir, Katingan Tengah, Pulau Malan, Central Kalimantan), pp. 2 and 8-9; Katingan was ISO 639-3 [kxg], retired 2008-01-14 and merged into Ngaju [nij] = Glottolog ngaj1237 (Glottolog kati1278 is bookkeeping). The catalog entry 'Dayak (Ngaju)' presumably refers to Ngaju proper (Kapuas/Kahayan/Pulopetak varieties), so the final-stress finding should be recorded as a Katingan-dialect statement under ngaj1237 rather than as a correction of the Ngaju record.

readall_conflicts: The catalog's StressTyp2 record gives Ngaju fixed penultimate stress. The one substantive new source read, Kaufman & Himmelmann (2024, submitted MS p. 4), instead suggests, on explicit auditory impression only, that Ngaju Dayak shows 'remarkably even prominence across syllables' and may belong to the stressless 'Java prototype' (citing Tadmor 2000 for lack of lexical accent as a general western Indonesian feature) — a different type from the catalog's fixed penult, but hedged and unverified. Ristati (2006, abstract only) says Ngaju has no suprasegmental phonemes, which is compatible with either a predictable penultimate rule or stresslessness and settles nothing about placement. A further complication outside the assigned list: the Balai Bahasa 'Tata Bahasa Dayak Ngaju' (2013, already held by the project as, section 2.6 'Fonem suprasegmental', p. 30) claims length and stress ('tekanan') are meaning-distinguishing suprasegmental phonemes, but its 'stress' examples ([papaʔ] 'kotor' vs [papak] 'ketok', [hekaʔ] vs [hekak], etc.) are final glottal-stop vs /k/ contrasts, not stress contrasts, so that claim does not support contrastive stress and conflicts with Ristati's 'no suprasegmental phonemes'. audit.reasoning: Both deciding quotations are verbatim in copies we hold at the cited places (Hardeland 1858:18-19, confirmed by page marker and heading; Mihing & Stokhof 1977:55 sec. 3.3.3, confirmed by re-scanned of the scan we hold's page 7 showing folio 55). The classification rests on the language's only full reference grammar plus an independent 1977 phonology article on a named dialect, 120 years apart, agreeing on penultimate, non-contrastive stress; the database entries (StressTyp2, Gordon 2002) derive from the same 1977 article we hold. Nothing better exists in Glottolog's list: the openly available Indonesian sketches (1991, 2013, downloaded now) are silent or confused on stress, and Ristati 2006 is an unpublished MA thesis. sources.quote: "Every word has the accent on only one syllable. It falls, as the many examples given above show, on the penultimate syllable, which as a rule is also the main syllable of the stem word. Where, however, in words derived by suffixes this main syllable becomes the antepenult, the accent nevertheless remains on the penultima, thus shifting from the originally stressed syllable onto the (formerly) unstressed syllable of the stem." Contoh: [kàwìlâp] 'bilah' [bàgàmbûh] 'rakus' [bàsèpût] 'gemuk' [hàntùÊn] 'kuntilanak' ... [p.97] Tekanan yang dikenakan pada kata bersuku empat ini umumnya sedang menuju agak keras. Contoh: [tàbàlîÈn] 'kayu ulin' [kùwàltûtàl] 'gagap' [kàmàsârày] 'serai' [jàlàtîÈn] 'sembilan' ... Berdasarkan data yang diperoleh, dalam bahasa Katingan tidak ditemukan tekanan yang membedakan makna (distingtif).
sources.locator: Bab II sec. 2.8 'Unsur Suprasegmental', 2.8.1 'Tekanan', printed pp. 95-97 (pp. 112-114); restated in Bab V conclusion, printed p. 135 (p. 152)
sources.note: Book-length phonology of the Katingan dialect of Ngaju; Pusat Bahasa phonologies usually carry a 'tekanan' section, giving a third dialect point (record rests on Pulau Petak 1977 and Hardeland's Kapuas/Pulopetak 1858).
